description: Everything inside a broker: where request time goes (queue / local / remote / response), thread pool saturation, purgatory, replication, ISR changes, connections and the log layer. Select one or more brokers and request types at the top.

panels.description: Broker state from kafka.server:type=KafkaServer,name=BrokerState per selected broker. 'running' (3) is healthy; starting/recovering after restarts; shutting down during rolling updates.
panels.title: Broker state

panels.description: Partition leaders on the selected brokers. Leaders do the client work: balance them across brokers.
panels.title: Leaders

panels.description: Under-replicated partitions led by the selected brokers.
panels.title: Under-replicated

panels.description: Average idle share of the request handler threads (lowest selected broker). < 20 % = saturated.
panels.title: Handler idle

panels.description: Average idle share of the network threads (lowest selected broker). < 30 % = add network threads.
panels.title: Network idle

panels.description: Open client and inter-broker connections on the selected brokers.
panels.title: Connections

panels.description: How long the JMX exporter needed to collect the metrics of the slowest selected broker. It runs inside the broker JVM: keep it well below the scrape interval (alert at 25 %). See docs/metrics-performance-impact.md.
panels.title: JMX scrape time

panels.description: Kafka handles a request in five phases: 1 waiting in the request queue for an I/O thread (high = handler threads saturated), 2 local processing on the leader (high = slow disk/page cache misses), 3 remote: waiting for followers (acks=all) or in purgatory for fetch.min.bytes / fetch.max.wait.ms, 4 waiting in the response queue for a network thread, 5 sending the response (high = slow clients or network). Percentiles are per phase and therefore not strictly additive — the tallest band is the bottleneck.
panels.title: Where does $request time go? (p99 per phase)

panels.description: Total request time percentiles reported by the broker (Yammer histograms with a decaying 5-minute reservoir). The gap between p50 and p99 shows how spiky latency is; compare with the phase breakdown to see which phase causes the tail.
panels.title: $request total time p50 / p99 / p99.9

panels.description: Requests per second per API key on the selected brokers (summed over API versions). Use it to correlate latency changes with load changes.
panels.title: Request rate by type

panels.description: Time requests were delayed by client quotas (produce/fetch/request quotas). Non-zero only if quotas are configured and a client exceeds them — then the client, not the broker, is the bottleneck.
panels.title: Throttle time p99

panels.description: Share of time the request handler threads (num.io.threads) were idle, computed from the idle-time meter over the selected interval. Healthy > 40 %; < 20 % means requests wait in the request queue. Broker and controller pools are shown separately on combined nodes.
panels.title: Request handler (I/O thread) idle

panels.description: Share of time the network threads (num.network.threads) were idle. Below 30 % the broker cannot read requests / write responses fast enough; raise num.network.threads or reduce connections.
panels.title: Network processor idle

panels.description: Requests waiting for an I/O thread (request queue, bounded by queued.max.requests) and responses waiting for a network thread. Should hover near 0; a growing request queue is the leading indicator of handler saturation.
panels.title: Request / response queue size

panels.description: Idle ratio of the new group coordinator runtime threads (KIP-848) and its event queue size. Low idle with a growing queue means offset commits and heartbeats are delayed — consumer rebalances get slow.
panels.title: Group coordinator threads idle

panels.description: Time events wait in, and are processed by, the controller event queue on nodes with the controller role (p99). High values delay leader elections and broker registrations — see KRaft Controller & Quorum.
panels.title: Controller event queue (this node)

panels.description: Delayed operations parked until a condition is met: Produce waits for follower acknowledgements (acks=all), Fetch waits for fetch.min.bytes or fetch.max.wait.ms. A large Fetch purgatory is normal with long-polling consumers; a growing Produce purgatory means followers are slow.
panels.title: Requests waiting in purgatory

panels.description: Delayed operations that are still pending (purgatory size also counts completed but not yet purged ones). Compare Produce here with the produce 'remote' phase above.
panels.title: Delayed operations (not yet completed)

panels.description: Partitions led by this broker whose followers are lagging (under-replicated) or below min.insync.replicas. The broker that LEADS the partitions reports them — the slow FOLLOWER is usually another broker: check the replica fetcher lag below.
panels.title: Under-replicated / under-min-ISR per broker

panels.description: Rate of in-sync replica set changes. Shrinks without matching expands = replicas fall out and do not come back. Correlate with GC pauses (JVM) and disk latency (Pods & Nodes).
panels.title: ISR shrinks / expands per broker

panels.description: Largest lag (in messages) of any partition this broker replicates as a follower. Should stay close to 0; a broker that cannot keep up shows a growing line here. Dead fetcher threads or failed partitions are shown as separate series when non-zero.
panels.title: Replica fetcher max lag

panels.description: Partition leaders and replicas hosted by each broker. Leaders carry the client traffic, so an uneven leader count means uneven load; run a preferred leader election or Cruise Control if one broker leads much more than the others.
panels.title: Leaders and replicas per broker

panels.description: Bytes this broker fetched as follower (in) and served to followers (out). Reassignment traffic is shown separately when a reassignment is running.
panels.title: Replication bytes per broker

panels.description: Client and inter-broker connections per listener. Every client instance opens connections to the brokers it talks to; thousands of connections or a sawtooth pattern indicate connection churn (short-lived clients).
panels.title: Open connections by listener

panels.description: New and closed connections per second per broker. Steady high rates (connection storms) cost CPU for TLS/SASL handshakes and are a classic cause of high network-thread load.
panels.title: Connection creation / close rate

panels.description: Bytes received and sent by the socket server per listener (client, replication and controller listeners separately).
panels.title: Network bytes by listener

panels.description: Failed SASL/TLS authentications per second. Non-zero values mean misconfigured clients or someone guessing credentials.
panels.title: Failed authentications

panels.description: Fraction of time network threads spend doing I/O (io-ratio) versus waiting for I/O (io-wait-ratio), averaged per listener.
panels.title: Network thread I/O ratio

panels.description: Error codes returned per request type. See the Kafka protocol docs for each code; NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER and FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH are benign during leader changes.
panels.title: Error responses (excluding NONE)

panels.description: Requests that failed inside the broker and records rejected for being invalid (bad CRC, wrong magic, out-of-order sequence for idempotent producers) or too large (bytes rejected, see message.max.bytes).
panels.title: Failed produce / fetch requests and rejected records

panels.description: Time to fsync a log segment (p50/p99) and flushes per second. Kafka normally relies on the page cache and flushes rarely; high flush latency means the disk is saturated — produce latency (local phase) follows.
panels.title: Log flush latency

panels.description: Log directories the broker marked offline after an I/O error. Any non-zero value means partitions on that disk are unavailable on this broker.
panels.title: Offline log directories

panels.description: Compaction health: the dirtiest log's dirty ratio and uncleanable partitions. Partitions become uncleanable after errors; then compacted topics grow forever.
panels.title: Log cleaner (compaction)

panels.description: Fetch session cache: sessions and cached partitions (KIP-227) and evictions. Evictions > 0 mean max.incremental.fetch.session.cache.slots is too small, causing full fetch requests (more CPU and bandwidth).
panels.title: Incremental fetch sessions
